post.script: At this spot, the closest humans are usually in space. It's called Point Nemo, the place in the ocean farthest from any land. The nearest shore is about 2,700 kilometers away. But the International Space Station orbits only about 400 kilometers above Earth. So when it flies overhead, astronauts are the closest people to you. And it gets creepier. Space agencies use this exact spot as a graveyard for old spacecraft. Hundreds of satellites and space station parts now lie on the sea floor down there. Which makes it the loneliest place on Earth... watched from space.

post.script: In 1859, the Sun set telegraph machines on fire. On September 1st, astronomer Richard Carrington saw a blinding flash on the Sun. Hours later, the biggest solar storm ever recorded slammed into Earth. Auroras lit up the sky as far south as the Caribbean. Some people woke up and started making breakfast, thinking it was morning. Telegraph operators got electric shocks, and some machines threw sparks. Some kept working even with their batteries disconnected, powered by the storm itself. Scientists warn that a storm that big today could knock out power grids around the world.

post.script: There's a moon that sprays its ocean into space. It's called Enceladus, one of Saturn's moons, and it's covered in ice. In 2005, NASA's Cassini spacecraft spotted giant jets shooting from its south pole. They're water, blasting out from a hidden ocean under the ice. Cassini later flew straight through these plumes and tasted them. It found salt, organic molecules, and signs of hydrothermal activity, like vents on Earth's seafloor. On Earth, places like that are packed with life. Which makes this tiny moon one of the best places to look for aliens.

post.script: Two billion years ago, planet Earth built its own fully functional nuclear reactor. In 1972, French physicists testing uranium ore from Gabon discovered something impossible. The concentration of fissile uranium-235 was depleted, exactly like spent fuel from modern power plants. At first, researchers feared someone had secretly manufactured atomic material in prehistoric Africa. But that's not the strangest part... Natural groundwater had trickled into rich uranium deposits, slowing neutrons and igniting spontaneous nuclear chain reactions. For hundreds of thousands of years, these subterranean reactors generated continuous thermal power without melting down. Which makes you realize that long before human civilization existed...

post.script: This frog makes itself invisible by hiding its own blood. It's called the glass frog, and from underneath you can see its heart beating. But red blood should give it away. So how does it vanish while it sleeps? In 2022, scientists finally found out. When it falls asleep, it pulls almost ninety percent of its red blood cells out of circulation and packs them inside its liver. Its body becomes up to three times more see-through. And here's the part scientists still can't explain. Packing that much blood together should cause deadly clots... but it doesn't. Which is why doctors are studying this tiny frog that hides its own blood.

post.script: This fish can turn a cup of water into a bucket of slime in under a second. Meet the hagfish. It has no jaw, no real spine, and it's been around for hundreds of millions of years. When a shark bites it, the hagfish releases a tiny amount of slime. That slime expands in seawater, thousands of times its size, almost instantly. It clogs the shark's gills, and the shark spits it out, gagging. To clean itself, the hagfish ties its own body into a knot and slides it down to scrape the slime off. Ugly? Maybe. But it's survived longer than the dinosaurs.
